Medicine-03.question: ১) Diseases associated with mosquito bite excludes..
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is amoebiasis. Amoebiasis is a food- and water-borne infection caused by Entamoeba histolytica, not transmitted by mosquitoes.

Mosquito-borne diseases:

  • Malaria → Plasmodium species (female Anopheles mosquito)

  • Dengue fever → Dengue virus (Aedes mosquito)

  • Filariasis → Filarial worms (mosquito vector)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Malaria → Transmitted by female Anopheles mosquito.

  • Dengue fever → Transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti mosquito.

  • Filariasis → Transmitted by mosquitoes carrying filarial larvae.

High-yield vector-borne diseases:

Disease Vector
Malaria Female Anopheles
Dengue Aedes
Filariasis Mosquito
Amoebiasis Contaminated food/water

Exam pearl:
Amoebiasis is not mosquito-borne.

Medicine-03.question: ২) “Break-bone fever” is characteristics of which of the following viral infection?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is dengue. “Break-bone fever” is a classic description of dengue fever due to severe myalgia, arthralgia, and bone pain.

Key features of dengue:

  • High fever

  • Severe headache

  • Retro-orbital pain

  • Severe muscle and joint pain (“break-bone fever”)

  • Rash

  • Thrombocytopenia

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Cytomegalovirus (CMV) → Causes mononucleosis-like illness, especially in immunocompromised patients.

  • EBV → Causes infectious mononucleosis (fever, pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy).

  • Mumps → Causes painful parotid swelling.

High-yield viral clues:

Disease Classic feature
Dengue Break-bone fever
EBV Pharyngitis + lymphadenopathy
CMV Mononucleosis-like syndrome
Mumps Parotitis

Exam pearl:
Break-bone fever = Dengue infection.

Medicine-03.question: ৩) Which of the following features suggest severe dengue?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is gastrointestinal haemorrhage. Severe dengue is characterised by severe bleeding, severe plasma leakage, and severe organ involvement.

Features suggesting severe dengue:

  • Severe bleeding → e.g., gastrointestinal haemorrhage

  • Severe plasma leakage leading to:

    • Shock

    • Pleural effusion

    • Ascites with respiratory distress

  • Severe organ involvement

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Abdominal pain/tenderness → Warning sign of dengue progression.

  • Persistent vomiting → Warning sign.

  • Pleural effusion or ascites → Suggests plasma leakage, but becomes a feature of severe dengue mainly when associated with respiratory distress or shock.

High-yield dengue classification:

Category Features
Dengue warning signs Abdominal pain, persistent vomiting, fluid accumulation
Severe dengue Severe bleeding, shock, severe organ dysfunction

Exam pearl:
Severe dengue = severe bleeding + severe plasma leakage + severe organ involvement.

Medicine-03.question: ৪) Which feature develop on the 2nd week of enteric fever?
৫) Treatment of enteric fever should be continued for how many days?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is 14 days. Antibiotic treatment for enteric (typhoid) fever is generally continued for about 10–14 days depending on the antibiotic used and clinical response. The classic exam answer is 14 days.

Common treatment durations:

  • Ceftriaxone → usually 10–14 days

  • Azithromycin → about 7 days (depending on regimen)

  • Fluoroquinolones → longer courses may be required depending on sensitivity

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 7 days → May be adequate for some azithromycin regimens but not the standard general answer.

  • 10 days → Used with some regimens but less classic.

  • 21 days → Longer than usual.

Exam pearl:
Enteric fever antibiotic duration (classic MCQ) = 14 days.

Medicine-03.question: ৬) Which one of the following is the specific investigation for thyphoid fever?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is blood culture. Blood culture is the gold standard and specific diagnostic investigation for enteric (typhoid) fever, especially during the first week of illness.

Diagnostic tests:

  • Blood culture → Most specific; detects Salmonella Typhi

  • Stool culture → May become positive later (usually 2nd–3rd week)

  • Widal test → Serological test; limited specificity due to false positives

  • CBC → Non-specific finding (often leucopenia)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • CBC → Shows supportive findings but is not diagnostic.

  • Stool cultures → Can confirm infection but sensitivity is lower and usually positive later.

  • Widal test → Not a definitive test due to variable sensitivity and specificity.

High-yield typhoid diagnosis:

Test Role
Blood culture Gold standard / specific test
Stool culture Later confirmation
Widal test Supportive, less reliable

Exam pearl:
Specific investigation for typhoid fever = Blood culture.

Medicine-03.question: ৭) Cardinal feature of leprosy excludes..
Medicine-03.option1: Skin lesions, typically anaesthetic at tuberculoid end of spectrum
Medicine-03.option4: Acid-fast bacilli on skin smears or biopsy

Medicine-03.question: ৮) M. leprae has tropism for which type of cell?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is Schwann cells. Mycobacterium leprae has a strong tropism for Schwann cells of peripheral nerves, leading to nerve damage and sensory loss.

Effects of M. leprae infection:

  • Invasion of Schwann cells

  • Peripheral nerve inflammation and damage

  • Loss of sensation

  • Muscle weakness and deformities

The other options are incorrect because:

  • RBC → Not infected by M. leprae.

  • WBC → Macrophages can contain bacilli, especially in multibacillary leprosy, but the characteristic cellular target is Schwann cells.

  • Platelet → Not involved.

High-yield leprosy pathogenesis:

M. leprae → Schwann cell infection → peripheral nerve damage → anaesthesia + deformity

Exam pearl:
Leprosy has a special affinity for Schwann cells.

Medicine-03.question: ৯) Plasmodium falciparum is a...
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is parasite. Plasmodium falciparum is a protozoan parasite that causes the most severe form of malaria, including cerebral malaria.

Key points:

  • Belongs to Apicomplexa (protozoan parasites)

  • Transmitted by female Anopheles mosquito

  • Infects:

    • Liver cells (initial stage)

    • Red blood cells (blood stage)

Features of P. falciparum malaria:

  • Severe anaemia

  • Cerebral malaria

  • Blackwater fever

  • Multi-organ complications

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Virus → Causes diseases such as dengue and influenza.

  • Bacteria → Causes diseases such as typhoid and tuberculosis.

  • Fungus → Causes diseases such as candidiasis and tinea.

High-yield malaria organisms:

Species Important feature
Plasmodium falciparum Most severe malaria
P. vivax Relapse due to hypnozoites
P. malariae Quartan fever

Exam pearl:
Plasmodium falciparum = protozoan parasite causing malaria.

Medicine-03.question: ১০) Preferred therapy for severe malaria is..
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is artesunate. Intravenous artesunate is the preferred treatment for severe malaria, especially severe Plasmodium falciparum malaria.

Key points:

  • IV artesunate rapidly reduces parasite biomass

  • Has lower mortality and fewer adverse effects compared with quinine

  • Followed by a complete course of an artemisinin-based combination therapy (ACT) after clinical improvement

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Co-artemether → Used for uncomplicated malaria, not severe malaria.

  • Quinine → Previously used for severe malaria but now generally an alternative when artesunate is unavailable.

  • Chloroquine → Used only for chloroquine-sensitive malaria; not effective for severe P. falciparum malaria due to resistance.

High-yield malaria treatment:

Malaria type Preferred treatment
Severe malaria IV artesunate
Uncomplicated falciparum malaria ACT (e.g., artemether-lumefantrine)
Vivax malaria Chloroquine (where sensitive) + primaquine

Exam pearl:
Severe malaria = IV artesunate is the drug of choice.

Medicine-03.question: ১১) rK39 test is used for antigen detection for diagnosis of which of the following disease?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is Kala-azar (visceral leishmaniasis). rK39 immunochromatographic test detects antibodies against the recombinant K39 antigen of Leishmania donovani and is used for diagnosis of visceral leishmaniasis.

Key points:

  • Disease: Visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar)

  • Organism: Leishmania donovani

  • Vector: Sandfly (Phlebotomus)

  • rK39 detects anti-Leishmania antibodies

Clinical features of Kala-azar:

  • Prolonged fever

  • Massive splenomegaly

  • Hepatomegaly

  • Pancytopenia

  • Hyperpigmentation of skin (“black fever”)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Malaria → Diagnosed by peripheral blood smear or malaria antigen tests.

  • Dengue → Diagnosed by NS1 antigen, IgM/IgG antibodies.

  • Schistosomiasis → Diagnosed by detection of eggs in stool/urine or serology.

High-yield diagnostic tests:

Disease Specific test
Kala-azar rK39 test
Malaria Blood film / rapid antigen test
Dengue NS1 antigen
Schistosomiasis Egg detection

Exam pearl:
rK39 = Visceral leishmaniasis (Kala-azar).

Medicine-03.question: ১২) Amoebiasis is caused by which of the following organism?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is Entamoeba histolytica. Amoebiasis (amoebic dysentery) is caused by the protozoan parasite Entamoeba histolytica.

Key points:

  • Transmission: Feco-oral route through contaminated food and water

  • Infective form: Cyst

  • Disease manifestations:

    • Amoebic dysentery (bloody diarrhoea)

    • Liver abscess (extraintestinal infection)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Ancylostoma duodenale → Hookworm causing iron deficiency anaemia.

  • Ascaris lumbricoides → Roundworm causing intestinal obstruction and Loeffler syndrome.

  • Enterobius vermicularis → Pinworm causing perianal itching.

High-yield intestinal parasites:

Organism Disease
Entamoeba histolytica Amoebiasis
Ancylostoma duodenale Hookworm infection
Ascaris lumbricoides Ascariasis
Enterobius vermicularis Enterobiasis

Exam pearl:
Amoebiasis = Entamoeba histolytica.

Medicine-03.question: ১৩) Which of the following is not a first line anti TB drug?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is metformin. Metformin is an antidiabetic drug and has no role in tuberculosis treatment.

First-line anti-TB drugs (initial regimen):

  • Isoniazid (H)

  • Rifampicin (R)

  • Pyrazinamide (Z)

  • Ethambutol (E)

(Usually given as HRZE in the intensive phase.)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Isoniazid → First-line anti-TB drug.

  • Rifampicin → First-line anti-TB drug.

  • Ethambutol → First-line anti-TB drug.

High-yield TB drugs:

Category Drugs
First-line HRZE
Second-line Fluoroquinolones, aminoglycosides, linezolid

Exam pearl:
HRZE = first-line anti-TB therapy; Metformin is not an anti-TB drug.

Medicine-03.question: ১৪) HIV mainly transmits through which of the following route?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is anal intercourse. Sexual transmission, particularly receptive anal intercourse, carries the highest risk of HIV transmission among sexual practices due to the vulnerability of rectal mucosa.

Major routes of HIV transmission:

  • Sexual contact (highest overall globally)

    • Receptive anal intercourse = highest sexual risk

  • Blood exposure:

    • Sharing needles

    • Contaminated blood transfusion (where screening is inadequate)

  • Mother-to-child transmission:

    • Pregnancy, delivery, breastfeeding

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Blood transfusion → Can transmit HIV, but risk is extremely low where blood screening is effective.

  • Vaginal delivery → Can transmit HIV from mother to child, but it is not the main route of adult-to-adult transmission.

  • Sharing needles → A significant route among people who inject drugs, but not the highest-risk sexual route.

High-yield HIV transmission:

Route Risk
Receptive anal intercourse Highest sexual risk
Sharing needles High risk
Vaginal intercourse Moderate risk
Blood transfusion High if unscreened

Exam pearl:
Highest risk sexual exposure for HIV = receptive anal intercourse.

Medicine-03.question: ১৫) Features of primary HIV infection excludes..
১৬) Which organism commonly causes urethritis?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is Chlamydia. Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common cause of non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU).

Common causes of urethritis:

  • Chlamydia trachomatis → Most common cause of NGU

  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae → Causes gonococcal urethritis

  • Mycoplasma genitalium → Important cause of persistent/recurrent NGU

  • Trichomonas vaginalis → Less common cause

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Gonorrhoea → Common cause of urethritis but less common than chlamydia overall.

  • Trichomonas vaginalis → Can cause urethritis but is not the commonest.

  • Mycoplasmas → Can cause urethritis, especially M. genitalium, but less common.

High-yield STI urethritis:

Type Common organism
Non-gonococcal urethritis (NGU) Chlamydia trachomatis
Gonococcal urethritis Neisseria gonorrhoeae

Exam pearl:
Most common cause of urethritis = Chlamydia trachomatis.

Medicine-03.question: ১৭) Syphilis is caused by which of the folloing organism?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is Treponema pallidum. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the spirochete bacterium Treponema pallidum.

Stages of syphilis:

  • Primary syphilis → Painless chancre at the site of infection

  • Secondary syphilis → Generalised rash (including palms and soles), lymphadenopathy

  • Tertiary syphilis → Gummas, cardiovascular and neurological complications

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae → Causes gonorrhoea (urethritis, cervicitis).

  • Chlamydia trachomatis → Causes chlamydial urethritis, cervicitis, PID, and lymphogranuloma venereum.

  • Human papillomavirus (HPV) → Causes genital warts and cervical cancer.

High-yield STI organisms:

Disease Organism
Syphilis Treponema pallidum
Gonorrhoea Neisseria gonorrhoeae
Chlamydia Chlamydia trachomatis
Genital warts HPV

Exam pearl:
Syphilis = Treponema pallidum (spirochaete).

Medicine-03.question: ১৮) Which is the specific test for Syphilis?
১৯) Chancroid is a sexually transmitted infection caused by which of the folloing organism?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is Haemophilus ducreyi. Chancroid is a sexually transmitted infection caused by the gram-negative coccobacillus Haemophilus ducreyi.

Key features of chancroid:

  • Painful genital ulcer

  • Tender inguinal lymphadenopathy

  • Ulcer has:

    • Ragged edges

    • Purulent base

    • Bleeds easily

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neisseria gonorrhoeae → Causes gonorrhoea (urethritis, cervicitis).

  • Treponema pallidum → Causes syphilis (classically painless chancre).

  • Chlamydia trachomatis → Causes chlamydia, lymphogranuloma venereum, and urethritis.

High-yield genital ulcers:

Disease Organism Ulcer
Chancroid Haemophilus ducreyi Painful ulcer
Syphilis Treponema pallidum Painless ulcer
Genital herpes HSV Painful vesicles/ulcers

Exam pearl:
Chancroid = painful ulcer + Haemophilus ducreyi.

Medicine-03.question: ২০) Which of the following isa cell of of the adaptive immune system
২১) Which is not a phagocytic cell?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is lymphocyte. Lymphocytes are not phagocytic cells; they are mainly involved in adaptive immune responses.

Phagocytic cells:

  • Neutrophils → First-line phagocytes against bacteria

  • Monocytes → Enter tissues and become macrophages

  • Macrophages → Professional phagocytes and antigen-presenting cells

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Neutrophils → Major phagocytic cells of innate immunity.

  • Monocytes → Circulating phagocytic cells.

  • Macrophages → Tissue-resident phagocytes derived from monocytes.

High-yield immune cells:

Function Cells
Phagocytosis Neutrophils, Monocytes, Macrophages
Adaptive immunity Lymphocytes (T & B cells)

Exam pearl:
Lymphocyte = immune regulation; Neutrophil/macrophage = phagocytosis.

Medicine-03.question: ২২) Which one is a primary lymphoid organ?
২৩) Humoral immunity is mediated by which of the following cell?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is B lymphocyte. Humoral immunity is mediated by B lymphocytes, which differentiate into plasma cells to produce antibodies.

Key points:

  • B lymphocyte → Plasma cell → Antibody production

  • Provides humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity

  • Important against extracellular bacteria and toxins

The other options are incorrect because:

  • T lymphocyte → Responsible for cell-mediated immunity (helper T cells, cytotoxic T cells).

  • Neutrophil → Innate immune cell involved in phagocytosis.

  • Eosinophil → Innate immune cell involved in parasitic infections and allergic responses.

High-yield immunity:

Type of immunity Main cell
Humoral immunity B lymphocyte
Cell-mediated immunity T lymphocyte

Exam pearl:
B cells make antibodies → humoral immunity.

Medicine-03.question: ২৪) Which immunoglobulin can cross the placenta?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is IgG. IgG is the only immunoglobulin that can cross the placenta and provides passive immunity to the fetus.

Key points:

  • Placental transfer occurs via Fc receptors on syncytiotrophoblasts

  • Maternal IgG antibodies protect the newborn during the first few months of life

  • Important for protection against:

    • Bacterial toxins

    • Viruses

    • Encapsulated organisms

The other options are incorrect because:

  • IgA → Present mainly in mucosal secretions (saliva, tears, breast milk); does not cross placenta.

  • IgM → Largest immunoglobulin; cannot cross placenta due to its size. First antibody produced in primary immune response.

  • IgE → Involved in allergic reactions and parasitic infections; does not cross placenta.

High-yield immunoglobulins:

Immunoglobulin Key feature
IgG Crosses placenta
IgA Mucosal immunity
IgM First antibody produced
IgE Allergy & parasites

Exam pearl:
Placental antibody transfer = IgG.

Medicine-03.question: ২৫) Both ESR & CRP raised in which of the following condition?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is Crohn’s disease. Both ESR and CRP are commonly elevated in active inflammatory bowel disease, especially Crohn’s disease, due to systemic inflammation.

Key points:

  • ESR → Marker of chronic inflammation

  • CRP → Marker of acute-phase inflammation and correlates with disease activity

  • Crohn’s disease often causes significant systemic inflammatory response → ↑ ESR + ↑ CRP

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) → ESR is usually raised, but CRP is often normal unless there is infection or significant serositis.

  • Sjögren’s syndrome → ESR may be elevated, but CRP is not typically markedly raised.

  • Ulcerative colitis → Can also increase ESR and CRP during active disease, but Crohn’s disease is a classic association in this type of MCQ.

High-yield inflammatory markers:

Condition ESR CRP
Crohn’s disease (active) ↑ ↑
SLE flare ↑ Usually normal
Infection ↑ ↑

Exam pearl:
Raised ESR + raised CRP = active inflammatory disease (classically Crohn’s disease).

Medicine-03.question: ২৬) Which of the following is an example of type-II hypersensitivity?
২৭) Most common type of graft rejection?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is acute cellular rejection. Acute cellular rejection is the most common type of graft rejection, especially in solid organ transplantation.

Key points:

  • Occurs mainly days to months after transplantation

  • Mediated by T lymphocytes

  • Causes lymphocytic infiltration and injury to graft tissue

  • Often responds to immunosuppressive therapy (e.g., corticosteroids)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Hyperacute rejection → Occurs within minutes to hours due to pre-existing antibodies against donor antigens.

  • Acute vascular rejection → Antibody-mediated rejection affecting graft vessels; less common.

  • Chronic allograft failure → Occurs months to years later due to chronic immune-mediated vascular and fibrotic changes.

High-yield graft rejection:

Type Time Mechanism
Hyperacute Minutes–hours Preformed antibodies
Acute cellular Days–months T-cell mediated
Chronic Months–years Fibrosis + vascular changes

Exam pearl:
Most common graft rejection = Acute cellular rejection (T-cell mediated).

Medicine-03.question: ২৮) The presence of leucocytes and nitrites in urine is indicative of
২৯) Oliguria is defined as being present when less than which ammount of urine is passed per day?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is 400 ml. Oliguria is defined as urine output less than 400 mL per 24 hours in adults.

Definitions of urine output:

  • Normal urine output: ~800–2000 mL/day

  • Oliguria: <400 mL/day

  • Anuria: <100 mL/day

Clinical significance:

  • Commonly seen in:

    • Acute kidney injury (AKI)

    • Hypovolaemia

    • Shock

    • Urinary tract obstruction

The other options are incorrect because:

  • 200 ml → Closer to anuria range.

  • 300 ml → Not the standard adult definition.

  • 500 ml → Above the usual oliguria cut-off.

High-yield renal definitions:

Term Urine output
Oliguria <400 mL/day
Anuria <100 mL/day

Exam pearl:
Oliguria = urine output <400 mL in 24 hours.

Medicine-03.question: ৩০) Haematuria in dipstick test and WBC in Urine microscopy are indicative of which of the following condition?
৩১) Which of the following is not a feature of nephritic syndrome?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is polyuria. Nephritic syndrome is characterised by inflammation of the glomeruli, causing haematuria, reduced renal function, and fluid retention—not increased urine output.

Features of nephritic syndrome:

  • Haematuria (often with RBC casts)

  • Oliguria (reduced urine output)

  • Hypertension

  • Oedema and fluid retention

  • Reduced renal function

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Oedema and generalised fluid retention → Common due to reduced GFR and salt/water retention.

  • Haematuria → Hallmark feature due to glomerular inflammation.

  • Reduced renal function → Common due to impaired glomerular filtration.

High-yield comparison:

Feature Nephritic syndrome Nephrotic syndrome
Haematuria +++ Rare
Proteinuria Mild–moderate Massive
Oedema Present Marked
Urine output Oliguria Usually normal

Exam pearl:
Nephritic syndrome = haematuria + hypertension + oliguria; polyuria is not a feature.

Medicine-03.question: ৩২) Which one is a prominent feature of nephrotic syndrome?
৩৩) Which type of nephrotic syndrome is more common in children?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is minimal change disease (MCD). Minimal change disease is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.

Key points:

  • Common age group: Children (especially <10 years)

  • Pathology:

    • Normal light microscopy

    • Foot process effacement on electron microscopy

  • Usually responds well to corticosteroids

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) → Common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults; may also occur in children.

  • Membranous nephropathy → Common in adults, especially older patients.

  • Diabetic nephropathy → Common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults with diabetes.

High-yield nephrotic syndrome causes:

Age group Common cause
Children Minimal change disease
Adults FSGS, membranous nephropathy
Diabetes Diabetic nephropathy

Exam pearl:
Child with nephrotic syndrome → think Minimal Change Disease.

Medicine-03.question: ৩৪) Complication of nephrotic syndrome includes?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is All above. Nephrotic syndrome is characterised by heavy protein loss in urine, leading to hypoalbuminaemia, sodium retention, and hyperlipidaemia.

Features/complications of nephrotic syndrome:

  • Hypoalbuminaemia → Due to urinary loss of albumin.

  • Avid sodium retention → Due to renal sodium retention, contributing to oedema.

  • Hypercholesterolaemia → Increased hepatic lipoprotein synthesis in response to low plasma albumin.

Additional complications:

  • Increased risk of infections (loss of immunoglobulins)

  • Thrombosis (loss of anticoagulant proteins like antithrombin III)

  • Vitamin D deficiency

High-yield nephrotic syndrome:

Massive proteinuria → Hypoalbuminaemia → Oedema + Hyperlipidaemia

Exam pearl:
Nephrotic syndrome triad = Proteinuria + Hypoalbuminaemia + Oedema (with hyperlipidaemia).

Medicine-03.question: ৩৫) Which of the following is a pre-renal cause of AKI?
৩৬) Which is not a usual examination finding of pre-renal AKI?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is hypertension. Pre-renal AKI occurs due to reduced renal perfusion, usually from volume depletion or reduced effective circulating volume, so hypertension is not a typical finding.

Typical examination findings in pre-renal AKI:

  • Tachycardia → compensatory response to reduced circulating volume

  • Weight decrease → due to fluid loss/dehydration

  • Dry mucous membranes → sign of dehydration

  • Postural hypotension may be present

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Tachycardia → Common in hypovolaemia causing pre-renal AKI.

  • Weight decrease → Suggests fluid depletion.

  • Dry mucous membranes → A classic sign of dehydration.

High-yield pre-renal AKI clues:

Volume depletion → ↓ renal perfusion → pre-renal AKI

Signs:

  • Tachycardia

  • Dry mucosa

  • Reduced skin turgor

  • Weight loss

  • Hypotension

Exam pearl:
Pre-renal AKI usually presents with dehydration signs, not hypertension.

Medicine-03.question: ৩৭) CKD usually develops over a period of
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is years. Chronic kidney disease (CKD) develops gradually over months to years due to progressive and irreversible loss of renal function.

Key points:

  • CKD = abnormal kidney structure or function for >3 months

  • Progressive nephron loss occurs slowly

  • Common causes:

    • Diabetes mellitus

    • Hypertension

    • Chronic glomerulonephritis

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Days → Suggests acute kidney injury (AKI).

  • Weeks → More consistent with subacute renal injury.

  • Months → CKD may be recognised after months, but typically develops over a prolonged period.

High-yield AKI vs CKD:

Feature AKI CKD
Onset Days–weeks Months–years
Reversibility Often reversible Usually irreversible
Definition Acute fall in kidney function Abnormality >3 months

Exam pearl:
CKD = progressive renal damage over years.

Medicine-03.question: ৩৮) Early symptom of CKD is?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is nocturia. Early CKD commonly presents with nocturia due to impaired urinary concentrating ability of the kidneys.

Early features of CKD:

  • Nocturia

  • Polyuria (especially early stages)

  • Fatigue

  • Mild hypertension

The other options are incorrect because:

  • UTI → Not a typical early symptom of CKD.

  • Proteinuria → May indicate kidney damage and can be an early marker, but it is a laboratory finding, not usually an early symptom.

  • Haematuria → Suggests glomerular disease or urinary tract pathology rather than a general early CKD symptom.

High-yield CKD progression:

Early CKD → nocturia/polyuria
Advanced CKD → fatigue, pruritus, anaemia, uraemic symptoms

Exam pearl:
Early symptom of CKD = nocturia due to reduced concentrating ability.

Medicine-03.question: ৩৯) Which one is the most common cause of CKD?
৪০) Which one is the most common cause of anaemia in CKD?
Medicine-03.option2: Toxic effects of uraemia on marrow precursor cells
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is deficiency of erythropoietin. The most common cause of anaemia in chronic kidney disease (CKD) is reduced erythropoietin production due to loss of functioning renal tissue.

Mechanism:

  • Diseased kidneys produce less erythropoietin (EPO)

  • ↓ EPO → ↓ bone marrow RBC production

  • Results in normocytic normochromic anaemia

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Toxic effects of uraemia on marrow precursor cells → Contributes to anaemia but is not the main cause.

  • Reduced red cell survival → Occurs in CKD due to uraemic toxins but is a secondary factor.

  • Blood loss → May occur due to dialysis or platelet dysfunction but is not the commonest cause.

High-yield CKD anaemia:

CKD → ↓ EPO production → ↓ RBC production → Normocytic anaemia

Exam pearl:
Most common cause of anaemia in CKD = erythropoietin deficiency.

Medicine-03.question: ৪১) Followings are Essential amino acid, excludes?
৪২) Obesity is regarded as a..?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is pandemic. Obesity is considered a global pandemic because it affects populations worldwide across many countries and continents.

Definitions:

  • Pandemic → Disease/condition affecting populations across multiple countries or continents.

  • Epidemic → Increase of disease cases above expected levels in a particular community or region.

  • Outbreak → Sudden occurrence of cases in a limited area.

  • Cluster → Group of cases occurring closely in time and place.

High-yield epidemiology terms:

Term Meaning
Pandemic Global spread
Epidemic Regional increase
Outbreak Localised occurrence
Cluster Group of cases

Exam pearl:
Obesity = global pandemic (non-communicable disease).

Medicine-03.question: ৪৩) Among Asians, BMI > 25.5 indicates...
Medicine-03.exp: Explanation: among Asians, BMI > 23.0 is overweight and > 25.0 is obese.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৪) Which one is a water-soluble vitamin?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is Vitamin B. B-complex vitamins are water-soluble vitamins that dissolve in water and are not stored extensively in the body.

Water-soluble vitamins:

  • Vitamin B complex

  • Vitamin C

Fat-soluble vitamins:

  • Vitamin A

  • Vitamin D

  • Vitamin E

  • Vitamin K

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Vitamin A → Fat-soluble vitamin.

  • Vitamin D → Fat-soluble vitamin.

  • Vitamin E → Fat-soluble vitamin.

High-yield vitamins:

Type Vitamins
Water-soluble B, C
Fat-soluble A, D, E, K

Exam pearl:
Water-soluble vitamins = B and C.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৫) Which one is a rich source of vitamin C?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is citrus fruit. Citrus fruits are rich sources of vitamin C (ascorbic acid).

Rich sources of vitamin C:

  • Citrus fruits (orange, lemon, grapefruit)

  • Fresh fruits (especially guava, berries)

  • Fresh vegetables (especially peppers, broccoli)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Fresh fruit → Many contain vitamin C, but citrus fruits are a classic rich source.

  • Fresh and frozen vegetables → Can contain vitamin C but usually less emphasised as the best source.

  • Liver → Rich in vitamin A, iron, and vitamin B12, not vitamin C.

High-yield vitamin C:

Sources: Citrus fruits
Deficiency: Scurvy (bleeding gums, poor wound healing)

Exam pearl:
Vitamin C rich food = Citrus fruits.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৬) Defficiency of folate level is best assessed by which of the following invstigation?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is RBC folate level. Red cell folate reflects long-term folate status and is the best indicator of folate deficiency.

Key points:

  • RBC folate → Reflects folate stores over the lifespan of RBCs (~120 days)

  • Serum/plasma folate → Reflects recent dietary intake and fluctuates rapidly

The other options are incorrect because:

  • S. Ferritin → Assesses iron stores, not folate deficiency.

  • Plasma folate level → Can detect deficiency but is less reliable due to short-term variation.

  • Bone marrow folate level → Not used routinely for assessment.

High-yield folate assessment:

Test Significance
RBC folate Best assessment of folate status
Serum folate Recent intake

Exam pearl:
Best investigation for folate deficiency = RBC folate level.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৭) Deficiency of which vitamin causes night blindness?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is Vitamin A. Vitamin A deficiency causes night blindness (nyctalopia) due to impaired function of retinal photoreceptors.

Key points:

  • Vitamin A is required for formation of rhodopsin in rod cells of the retina.

  • Deficiency causes:

    • Night blindness

    • Xerophthalmia

    • Bitot spots

    • Keratomalacia (severe cases)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Vitamin B → Deficiency causes conditions like neuropathy (B1), anaemia (B12/folate), dermatitis (B3), etc.

  • Vitamin C → Deficiency causes scurvy.

  • Vitamin D → Deficiency causes rickets and osteomalacia.

High-yield vitamin deficiencies:

Vitamin Deficiency feature
Vitamin A Night blindness
Vitamin B12 Megaloblastic anaemia, neuropathy
Vitamin C Scurvy
Vitamin D Rickets/osteomalacia

Exam pearl:
Night blindness = Vitamin A deficiency.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৮) Wernicke’s encephalopathy is caused by which of the following vitamin deficiency?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is Thiamin (Vitamin B1). Wernicke’s encephalopathy occurs due to thiamine deficiency, commonly seen in chronic alcohol misuse.

Classic features of Wernicke’s encephalopathy:

  • Confusion

  • Ophthalmoplegia (eye movement abnormalities)

  • Ataxia

Pathophysiology:

  • Thiamine is required for glucose metabolism in the brain.

  • Deficiency leads to neuronal injury, especially in the mammillary bodies and periaqueductal grey matter.

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Riboflavin (Vitamin B2) → Deficiency causes cheilosis, angular stomatitis, and glossitis.

  • Niacin (Vitamin B3) → Deficiency causes pellagra (dermatitis, diarrhoea, dementia).

  • Pyridoxine (Vitamin B6) → Deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy and sideroblastic anaemia.

High-yield vitamin B deficiencies:

Vitamin Deficiency manifestation
B1 (Thiamin) Wernicke’s encephalopathy, beriberi
B2 (Riboflavin) Cheilosis, glossitis
B3 (Niacin) Pellagra
B6 (Pyridoxine) Neuropathy, sideroblastic anaemia

Exam pearl:
Wernicke’s encephalopathy = Vitamin B1 (Thiamin) deficiency.

Medicine-03.question: ৪৯) which of the following is required for synthesis of thyroid hormones?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is iodine. Iodine is an essential component of thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) and is required for their synthesis.

Key points:

  • Thyroid follicular cells trap iodide from blood.

  • Iodine is incorporated into thyroglobulin to form:

    • T3 (triiodothyronine)

    • T4 (thyroxine)

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Calcium → Important for bone health and muscle function, not thyroid hormone synthesis.

  • Iron → Required for many enzymes, but not a structural component of thyroid hormones.

  • Sodium → Important for fluid balance; iodide transport into thyroid uses the sodium-iodide symporter, but sodium itself is not required for hormone structure.

High-yield thyroid hormone synthesis:

Iodine + Tyrosine (in thyroglobulin) → T3 and T4

Exam pearl:
Essential element for thyroid hormone synthesis = Iodine.

Medicine-03.question: ৫০) Which of the following is the most abundant cation in the body?
Medicine-03.exp:
The correct answer is calcium. Calcium is the most abundant cation in the human body, with approximately 99% stored in bones and teeth.

Key points:

  • Total body calcium ≈ 1–1.2 kg

  • Functions:

    • Bone and teeth formation

    • Muscle contraction

    • Nerve transmission

    • Blood coagulation

The other options are incorrect because:

  • Iron → Essential trace element involved in haemoglobin synthesis, but present in much smaller amounts.

  • Iodine → Trace element required for thyroid hormone synthesis.

  • Sodium → Most abundant extracellular cation, but not the most abundant cation in the whole body.

High-yield electrolytes:

Category Most abundant
Total body cation Calcium
Extracellular fluid cation Sodium
Intracellular fluid cation Potassium

Exam pearl:
Most abundant cation in the body = Calcium; most abundant extracellular cation = Sodium.
